attempts.name: g1a1
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-trace rule as the main signal and added three general signals. Production frames are now ranked by their position in each trace (top of stack first) and summed across failing tests. The failure message and string literals in the test's window are matched against production lines using IDF-weighted word overlap, which finds the code that produces the expected text, such as the `"Missing required options"` literal in the cli case. Identifiers in the test body and the top production file's references to other production classes add lower-weight candidates at their class declarations, which targets fixes spread over several files. Picks within 25 lines of each other in one file are merged so the six slots cover different places. I have not run this against the training cases, so the weights are untuned guesses.

attempts.name: g1a2
attempts.notes: The previous answer was cut off mid-module, so this version is shorter. It keeps the stack-frame rule and adds two signals: identifiers from the failing test body and report messages, weighted by rarity across production files, and one hop to classes that the top files reference. Line choice smooths evidence over a small window, skips blank and comment lines, and spreads picks across files with a penalty for repeats. The module is untested; I checked the logic by reading it, not by running it against the training cases.

attempts.name: g1a3
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-trace rule as the backbone and added three signals the misses point to. First, production frames are still ranked top-first, but their scores now decay with depth. Second, when a test frame is in the trace, the identifiers on that test line (called methods and capitalized type names) are resolved to production declarations, since the test line often names the code under change even when the trace never enters it. Third, words from the failing test's name are matched against production method and class names, as a weaker tie-breaker. Candidates are deduplicated so that no two returned entries in the same file are within 40 lines of each other, which spreads the six slots across distinct edit regions. Nothing here is tied to a particular project, class or test.

attempts.name: g1a4
attempts.notes: I added three general signals to the stack-trace rule, since most misses in the examples touch files that never appear in a trace. First, production methods that the failing test calls, on the failing assertion line (strong) and in the lines just above it (weaker), are candidates at their declaration lines. Second, production files whose identifiers share words with the failure message and the failing test's method name are candidates, each at its best-matching declaration. Third, the top-ranked trace frames keep the top priority. Scoring is greedy and diverse: no two returned entries lie within 40 lines of each other in the same file, so the six slots cover different places. Method names declared in more than eight production places are ignored as too generic. The module is untested against the training cases; I reasoned about the examples rather than running them.

attempts.name: g2a1
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-frame backbone and the test-called-method and message-word signals, which were the only ones that helped in earlier generations. I added two general rules aimed at the misses where the edit lies in a file no trace names: the method enclosing each top production frame is a candidate, and so are declarations in other project classes that the frame method calls by name, one reference hop away. I also wrapped the whole run so an unexpected error returns an empty list rather than an exception. I have not run this against the training cases, so its effect on the score is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g2a2
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-frame ranking, the test-called-method signal, and the message-word matching, and added two general signals. First, the production methods named in the top frames are searched for call sites in other production files, since a bug often sits in a caller that passes bad arguments or skips a check. Second, each production file contributes at most two picks, so the six slots spread across files rather than piling into the first file that matches. The module has not been run against the training cases, so treat its score as unknown.

attempts.name: g2a3
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-trace backbone and the test-call and message-word signals, and changed three things. Production frames now decay in score with depth, since the top frames are the most likely edit sites. Each frame also contributes the declaration that encloses its line, because fixes often land at method starts. Finally, the top frame's file gets one hop: production files it references by type name are candidates when they share words with the failure message. I have not run this against the training cases, so the gain is unverified.

attempts.name: g2a4
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-frame backbone and the test-call and message-word signals from attempt 4, and added three general ones. Production string literals that also appear in the failing test's assertion or window now point to their production sites, since the expected text often comes from the code being fixed. Each top production frame also contributes its enclosing method's declaration, because long methods can put the real edit more than 40 lines from the frame. Finally, the production class matching the test class's name gets a weak candidate at its declaration. These additions are untested here, and I did not run the module on the training cases.

attempts.name: g3a1
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-frame backbone, the test-called-method signal and the message-word matching, since they were the only signals that helped in earlier generations. The one addition is a general rule for long methods: each top production frame also contributes the declaration of its enclosing method, scored just below the frame itself. The greedy window filter drops that candidate when the frame is already within 40 lines of it, so it only takes a slot when the enclosing method starts far from the frame. I also made the frame lookup use a sorted index. I have not run this against the training cases, so treat it as an unverified change.

attempts.name: g3a2
attempts.notes: I kept the stack-frame backbone and the test-called-method and message-word signals, since those are the only ones earlier generations showed to help. I added two general rules. First, a quoted string from the failing assertion or the expected text in the message, when it overlaps a string literal in production code, points to that production line, which covers cases where the expected text is built in the code being fixed. Second, a class name that appears in the message or the failing test's body, and matches a production file, contributes that class's declaration line. Neither rule has been run against the training cases, so the gain is unverified.

attempts.name: g3a3
attempts.notes: I added a subject-class signal. Production files whose names match the test class (for example `BrentSolverTest` maps to `BrentSolver`) are the likeliest edit sites, and in the training misses that is a recurring pattern. Inside each such file, I rank method bodies by how many identifiers they share with the methods the failing test calls, plus IDF-weighted overlap with the failure-message words. The best two bodies become candidates at a score just under the test-called-method signal. The rest of the pipeline is unchanged, and the module has not been run against the training cases, so treat the gain as a hypothesis.

attempts.name: g3a4
attempts.notes: I added one general signal to the promoted generation-1 module: when a failing test's class is named after a production class (`FooTest` or `TestFoo` for `Foo`), the production methods that the failing test calls are also scored in that class's file. The old module already scored called methods by name across the whole project, so this only boosts the subject-class copies. I have not run it on the training set, so its effect is unmeasured. The rest of the module is unchanged.

attempts.name: g4a1
attempts.notes: I kept the promoted generation-3 module (65/198 on training) and changed only the parts that are safe to change without running it. I removed a dead expression that evaluated `tstem_name_of` only by accident, collapsed duplicate work in the test-class collection, and wrapped the whole run so an unexpected error falls back to a simple subject-file guess instead of an empty answer. I also padded short answers with the subject files' top method declarations, so unused slots are not wasted. None of this is a new localization signal, and I have not run it, so I expect little or no change on the training set. Earlier attempts that added signals mostly failed, so the next real gain probably needs a different kind of evidence than string or identifier overlap.

attempts.name: g4a2
attempts.notes: I changed one signal: how test-called method names are resolved to production declarations. Earlier versions dropped any called name with more than eight declarations. Those are often the names that matter most, such as overloaded helpers. Now every called name is kept, and its declarations are ranked by how many leading directories they share with the failing test's file. The top three are taken, and names with many declarations get a lower score. The rest of the module is unchanged. I have not run it on the training cases, so its effect is unmeasured. The main reason to expect a gain is that the training misses include edits in same-package files that the test calls by a common name.

attempts.name: g4a3
attempts.notes: The main change is a new signal: production classes that the failing test file references by name (imports, type names, constructors) are now candidates. Their declarations that the failing test calls score highest, followed by declarations sharing words with the failure message. The module also drops a leftover `if False` expression and an unused variable. I have not run this on the training cases, so its effect is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g4a4
attempts.notes: The change is a small tie-break in the stack-frame signal. When a production frame lies in a file named after the failing test's subject class (for example `BrentSolverTest` and `BrentSolver.java`), its score gets a boost, so such frames rank above frames in unrelated classes. The subject-class lookup now runs before the frame scoring, and the stray conditional expression is gone. I have not run this against any cases, so its effect is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g5a1
attempts.notes: I made one general change and removed a leftover dead expression. The top production frame's package siblings are now candidates when their names and declarations share words with the failure message. I added a shared `_best_decls` helper so declaration ranking is written once. Like the earlier attempts, this is unmeasured, and the training score has not moved from 65/198 in any run I can see. The dead `if False` expression is gone, and the test-class lookup is now a plain expression.

attempts.name: g5a2
attempts.notes: I kept the promoted generation-3 module, removed its dead `if False` expression, and made one change: production frames are now ordered so that frames in files hit by several trace frames come first. A file that appears repeatedly in a failure trace is more likely to hold the edit than one that appears once. I have not run this against any cases, so its effect is unmeasured. The rest of the logic is unchanged.

attempts.name: g5a3
attempts.notes: I changed very little, and I have not run this module, so its score is unmeasured. The previous generations all landed at 55–66 of 198 on training, and none of their writer's notes showed a gain I could reproduce. Given that, I kept the signals that earlier generations reported as useful and removed the defects I could see. The `if False` conditional that evaluated an undefined helper is gone, and the test-class collection is simplified to a direct filename lookup. The fallback path and the 40-line diversity filter are unchanged. The module should therefore behave like generation 3 attempt 3, the promoted version, minus its dead code. I did not add a new signal, because the missed cases shown here (a field declaration, a missing method-level edit in a file outside the trace, a comment-adjacent line) do not point to a general rule I could justify without running the training set.

attempts.name: g5a4
attempts.notes: I kept the generation-3 structure and made three changes. Field declarations (such as `public static final CSVFormat MYSQL = ...`) are now indexed alongside methods. Identifiers on the failing assertion line and the lines just above it are matched against those declarations, not only called names, because several misses hinge on a constant or field the assertion reads. I also removed the `if False` leftover and sorted every set before iteration, since string-set order changes with the hash seed and would make answers vary between runs. I have not run this against the training cases, so its effect is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g6a1
attempts.notes: I kept the generation-3 structure, which scored best on training, and made three changes that are safe to make without running it. I removed the leftover `tstem_name_of(t) if False else` expression and the dead `called_all` assignment. I also sorted the test-class set and the common-word set before iterating, so the output does not depend on the hash seed. Set iteration order affected which subject files were kept when more than three existed, and which word was picked as the fallback. None of these changes should move the score much, and I have not run the module, so its effect is unmeasured.

attempts.name: g6a2
attempts.notes: I kept the generation-3 structure, which is the promoted version at 65/198, and made only safe changes. I removed the dead `if False` conditional and replaced the test-class lookup with a direct filename derivation. I also sorted the test-class set before use, so the subject-file order no longer depends on the hash seed. Behavior should match the promoted module on any input where the old code ran cleanly. I have not run it, so its score is unmeasured, and I expect it to land near 65/198 rather than improve on it.

attempts.name: g6a3
attempts.notes: I kept the generation-3 structure and made one change: for the top production frames, the declaration that encloses each frame is now a candidate at a score just under the frames. A crash site often sits deep in a long method, and the method's head is a different, distant location the developers may also edit. The dedupe window still keeps the six slots spread out. I also removed the leftover `if False` expression and simplified the test-class collection. I have not run this module, so its effect on the training score is unmeasured. Earlier attempts have not moved the score past 65/198.

attempts.name: g6a4
attempts.notes: I made one small change and removed a dead expression. In the test-class collection, `tstem_name_of(t) if False else ...` always took the else branch, so I replaced it with the direct filename lookup. I also dropped the duplicate `called_all` assignment. The one behavioural change is that a production frame's enclosing method declaration is now a candidate when it differs from the frame line by more than a few lines. It is a weak signal, so I expect little effect. I have not run this module, so its training score is unmeasured and may match the current 65/198.
